speechtext: The hon. member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. Muir) is rising on a question of privilege. I wish to remind hon. members that according to the rules there should be an hour's written notice to the Chair. The hon. member, however, did send a written notice, and in view of the prevailing Christmas spirit I would think this should satisfy the rules of the house. I gather that the statement is to be of a brief nature.

subtopic: MR. MUIR (CAPE BRETON-THE SYDNEYS) - STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON INFLUENZA VACCINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege to draw attention to the statement
by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) on Tuesday, December 17, which can be found at page 4035 of Hansard regarding the Hong Kong influenza vaccine. The minister stated at that time:
We hope we will have a supply in Canada by mid January.
The fact of the matter is the vaccine is now available for selected cases. The aged and those suffering from certain illnesses have a priority. The vaccine is now being supplied by one of the research-based pharmaceutical organizations in the United States. It is my view that the statement by the minister might well mislead many people who should now be contacting their family doctors for the vaccine into not contacting their doctors until January. It may well be that the minister is today in a position to provide further information to the people. Naturally I hope this is the case. I feel also that the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard), a prominent physician in Canada, should be commended for his knowledge of the circumstances and for initially alerting the house and the country to the situation.
In conclusion I wish to quote from a letter that was forwarded to doctors on December 11 by Merck, Sharp and Dohme of Canada announcing the availability of the vaccine in question. The letter states:
Due to the limited supply of this product it is recommended that you give treatment priority to those persons with the highest risk of severe complications as a result of influenza.
If the minister needs any further convincing I have here a syringe and the vaccine, if he would like to have a shot.

ST. REGIS INDIANS-MOTION FOR COMMITTEE CONSIDERATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the provisions of standing order 42 read:
A motion may, in case of urgent and pressing necessity previously explained by the mover, be made by unanimous consent of the house without notice having been given under standing order 41.
I hope to take some action under that standing order by asking subsequently for the

December 19, 1968
Indian Treaty
unanimous consent of the house to present a particular motion and to precede it, as the standing order indicates, by explaining the reason for the motion in a very brief way.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
My reason for this arises from the arrest yesterday of more than 40 of the St. Regis people of the Iroquois nation near Cornwall, people who have suffered insouciance and indignities at the hands of the government for many, many years. High honour and high recognition were given to the Indians in the treaty signed between the United States and Great Britain in 1794, commonly known as Jay's treaty, which said that the Indian people had the right to cross the international border without paying customs duty. Perhaps I should read what the treaty says in article 3:
-nor shall Indians passing or repassing with their own proper goods and effects of whatever nature, pay for the same any import or duty whatever. But goods in bales or other large packages unusual among Indians shall not be considered goods belonging bona fide to Indians.
The government of Canada never presented this treaty to parliament for ratification, and as a consequence it has been held to have no force and effect. The Indian people concerned have waited patiently for the government to take some action ever since this decision by the Supreme Court was handed down a dozen years ago. The government also expropriated certain Indian lands in the Cornwall island area. Contingent upon that expropriation was the thought that an agreement would be reached with respect to it, but to date the government has not even had the common courtesy to make efforts toward such an agreement.
As a result of these and many other situations the people at St. Regis finally expressed their indignation yesterday by means of a demonstration which saw more than 40 of them arrested. In addition to these events the mayor of Cornwall is reported to have made a statement to the effect that the city of Cornwall had extended the boundaries of the city a dozen years ago to include Cornwall island; in other words that it is no longer reserve land, and that the people there might expect to receive taxation notices from the city shortly.
On this basis I should like to move:
That it be resolved by the House of Commons that it is urgent and expedient to authorize the standing committee on Indian affairs and northern development to meet forthhwith and proceed as quickly as possible to hear evidence on

1.	The document signed between the governments of the United States of America and Great Britain in 1794, commonly referred to as Jay's treaty, and the effect that this treaty has upon the Indian people as well as the matter of parliamentary action with respect to the treaty.
2.	The action of the government of Canada in expropriating certain lands of the people of the St. Regis Indian reserve for any purpose whatever.
3.	The relationship between the people of St. Regis and the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority or any other agency, branch or department of government.
4.	The matter of the city of Cornwall's claim that the St. Regis reserve has been annexed by that city, and
5.	Any other matter which the people of St. Regis deem it advisable to raise with the said committee.
And for the committee to report its findings and recommendations with all convenient speed and dispatch.

maintopic: TABLING OF INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT SIGNED TODAY
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: PROPOSED RATIFICATION OF NUCLEAR NONPROLIFERATION TREATY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon.
members will recall that on October 29 I tabled in the house copies of international treaties, agreements or protocols which Canada had signed or acceded to in recent months. Among those treaties was the nuclear nonproliferation treaty.
This treaty, which marked an important new step forward in arms control, was endorsed by the great majority of member states at a special session of the United Nations general assembly. It was then opened for signature in Washington, London and Moscow
December 19, 1968

on July 1. Canada signed the treaty in Washington and London on July 23 and in Moscow on July 27. More than 80 nations have now signed the treaty and three, Britain, Nigeria and Ireland, have ratified it. We hope that in due course all the nations of the world will recognize the importance of this treaty and accede to it.
Before the non-proliferation treaty comes into effect 43 states, including the three nuclear powers which have signed it, must deposit ratifications. We understand that the United States Senate will consider the question of ratification in January, and that the Soviet union will then make a decision regarding Russian ratification. As a leading proponent of the treaty and one of the major "near-nuclear" signatories, Canada has an opportunity to provide leadership by demonstrating our faith in the non-proliferation treaty. To do this we must take immediate steps to ensure that we are among the first to ratify. A positive decision by Canada may help to exert a favourable influence on other governments whose early support for the treaty is important to its future effectiveness.
The government therefore proposes to take the necessary action to permit Canadian ratification, if possible before the new year.
I am sure members on both sides of the house support the objectives for which this treaty was negotiated and will welcome the fact that the government of Canada now proposes to take steps to ratify it. I hope there will be opportunities in due course to discuss the treaty in the standing committee on external affairs and defence or when the estimates of the Department of External Affairs are under debate in the house. In order not to delay Canadian ratification, however, we would propose to move forward immediately. For this reason I am taking this opportunity to bring the matter to the attention of the house.
As a member of the 18-nation disarmament commitee Canada played an important role in negotiations during the last seven years which culminated in the presentation at the April, 1968 session of the United Nations general assembly of an agreed draft treaty designed to limit the spread of nuclear weapons. Our support for the principles embodied in this treaty has been unwavering. We continue to believe that without an agreement of this nature there is little prospect of progress toward controlling the dissemination of nuclear weapons or toward general disarmament.
Nuclear Arms Treaty
In effect the non-proliferation treaty will prohibit signatory countries not now in possession of nuclear weapons from manufacturing or otherwise acquiring such weapons and devices. It prohibits nuclear powers from transferring nuclear weapons or explosives to non-nuclear weapon states. It requires nonnuclear states to accept international safeguards on their nuclear programs but guarantees their rights to exploit nuclear energy for peaceful purposes and to obtain the benefits of peaceful nuclear explosions.
In my opinion the non-proliferation treaty is a significant contribution to the three basic objectives that guided Canadian participation in the lengthy negotiations that led to its conclusion. First, the treaty will reduce the sense of uncertainty and insecurity which aggravates international tensions, accelerates the arms race and increases the risk of nuclear war. It is thus a contribution toward long term world security. Second, the treaty represents an initial but essential step toward the control and reduction of existing stocks of nuclear weapons. Further steps forward are urgently required, and at this current session of the United Nations general assembly I welcomed indications that the United States and the Soviet union are discussing the initiation of talks on the limitation of strategic nuclear armed missile systems, including anti-ballistic missiles.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
Our third objective, that effective international safeguards be applied as widely as possible on all the processes involved in the nuclear field, is enhanced by this treaty. By extending and consolidating international safeguards procedures it should facilitate exchanges and co-operation in the peaceful uses of nuclear energy.
Members of the house will recognize, I am sure, that the full potential of the non-proliferation treaty can be realized only if it is respected and accepted by a very large majority of states. The Canadian decision to ratify will, we hope, play a major part in convincing additional countries of the necessity of bringing this treaty into force at the earliest possible date.

Mr. Speaker, I will endeavour not to proliferate words on this particular subject. I think everybody in the house welcomes the announcement that has been made. It is a step forward in the direction of security in the nuclear world. We all know there are many other things that must be done, but we have to take each step as it is available.
We believe this non-proliferation treaty can hardly have its full effect until the present nuclear nations take further steps. First of all there should be a ban on underground testing as well as on testing in the atmosphere. We believe moves should be made toward limiting the means of delivery of the present nuclear powers, and toward diminishing the stockpiles they have at the present time. There is need for greater security and for strengthening the United Nations.
All these steps are necessary if this treaty is to bring the security that is its purpose. But, as I said, we have to take one step at a time, and we welcome the treaty that Canada is to ratify. We will be very happy in the committee of external affairs and national defence to go into the details of this treaty.

Mr. Speaker, we are happy to comment the statement that the honourable Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) has just made with regard to nuclear weapons.
I am convinced that the whole world would like to see them disappear and the advancement of nuclear science put to the service of humanity. Nuclear weapons are considered by humanity as destructive weapons when they should be a power of resurrection.

Many countries of the world are stunned by the destructive power of these weapons knowing full well that they can destroy everything on earth. The peoples of the world have to yield to the will of the four great powers that have nuclear arms.
Mr. Speaker, instead of endeavouring to reduce the proliferation of nuclear arms, we should use all those new technological developments to serve humanity and help the economic development of the world.

subtopic: HOGS-ANNOUNCEMENT OF CHANGES IN GRADES AND PREMIUMS

speakeroldname: Hon. H. A. Olson (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: HOGS-ANNOUNCEMENT OF CHANGES IN GRADES AND PREMIUMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a brief statement about a change in hog premiums. A short time ago I announced changes in the grades and grading of hogs which will take place on December 30, 1968. The present grades of A, B and C will be replaced by an index scale based on the scientific principle of appraising carcass merit on the basis of back fat and weight measurements. Since the pricing policy of meat packers will be based on this premise, the immediate result will be a greater reward from the market place to the producer who sells hogs that yield a relatively high proportion of lean. The long term result will be an increase in the production of higher quality pork of the type the consumer wants.
To provide initial impetus to the attainment of this objective the hog premium is being altered to apply at a higher rate to fewer hogs. Commencing December 30, 1968 and until further notice, there will be paid a premium of $3 per hog carcass with an index of 103 or higher. This will be an increase per carcass from the present $2 premium for grade A carcasses, but as I stated earlier it will apply to a smaller percentage of hogs.
I am pleased to be able to report that this new system of hog carcass appraisal has been developed by representatives of producers and processors along with government officials working in close co-operation.

subtopic: HOGS-ANNOUNCEMENT OF CHANGES IN GRADES AND PREMIUMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the statement by the minister this afternoon with regard to a change in the grading program is very important to the industry concerned. At last the government is taking concrete action that will enable this industry to meet competition and world
December 19, 1968

demand for protein rather than carbohydrates and fat.
The minister stated the long term result will be an increase in the production of higher quality pork. When the minister states that the $3 instead of the former $2 will apply to a smaller percentage of hogs, what he is really saying is that in the years ahead the industry will receive from the government far less by way of payments, and this at a time when the industry needs those payments most.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
This is a concrete illustration of what can happen to an industry when the government lacks a long range policy. Within two weeks there will be a change in the payments made to the primary producers, when, had the government announced its intention 18 months or two years ago, it would have enabled the producers to take advantage of this change in the grade system. As it is now, definite hardship will be caused among the producers during the next six months to two years, depending on the particular production engaged in.

subtopic: HOGS-ANNOUNCEMENT OF CHANGES IN GRADES AND PREMIUMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this new grading system has been in the making for some time, and has been exhaustively researched. The federation of agriculture, the processors and so on have all taken part, and I think we will have to see how it works out in practice in the slaughter plants, whether it operates effectively on the production line and does not slow the product as it goes through. It will mean that premiums to some farmers who are now receiving them will be ruled out. Therefore I think the emphasis now will be on top grade hogs and producers of lower grade hogs will not receive any premium.
I think one area that has not been explored and researched in view of the proposals now made in the grade marking of quality hogs before they are passed on to the consumer. I think this top quality grading should be passed on from the farmer-producer to the ultimate consumer, as is the case now with beef. I did make this point in the committee on agriculture and was told that for certain reasons this cannot be done, but I think it can.
I do not think any objective examination was made into whether it can be done, and this is a real weakness in this new system. As I say, the main point here is that the quality product be passed on as such from the producer to the consumer.

subtopic: HOGS-ANNOUNCEMENT OF CHANGES IN GRADES AND PREMIUMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my opinion, the statement made
Statistics Act
by the Minister of Agriculture about the grading of hogs meets the need to encourage even more the production of higher quality pork.
That policy offers some advantages of course, but it also has some disadvantages, and I think that it will be necessary to proceed by stages in order to prevent too heavy losses for the producers who might produce hogs of a quality inferior to the standards that have just been announced in the house.
However, I ask myself a question which must have crossed the minister's mind and which might even have been discussed, although it was not mentioned in his statement. In view of special conditions in the province of Quebec where the government now pays a premium for grade A hogs, in order to help the producers even more, in view also of the fact that grades A and B will be abolished, will the Quebec government keep on grading hogs in the same way and paying the premium or has some agreement been reached? I presume that the federal Minister of Agriculture and his Quebec counterpart have considered the situation and, at the right moment, we would be happy to hear the minister's explanations.
At all events, it appears to us at first sight that this new policy will promote a higher quality production.
The other day, I heard an hon. member say that he was worried about the fact that farmers were not always concerned with quality. I think that this is a gratuitous assertion because even though it might have been so in the past, in 1968 farmers accept more and more to produce high quality products and meet the consumer needs, provided they are compensated for the quality of their products.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, December 16, consideration of the motion of Mr. Blair that the fourth report of the special committee on procedure of the house, presented to the house on Friday, December 6, be concurred in, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Stanfield (p. 3762).

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGraih (St. John's East):
subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FOURTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I adjourned the debate on December 16 I was referring to the difficulties that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and some of the members of the government were having in trying to distinguish between the deliberative function of parliament and the investigative function of committees of the house. I dwelt at some length on that subject because I think it is very important and germane to any discussion in this debate. The committees of the house as they are now constituted are by their very nature investigative

DEBATES	December 19, 1968
bodies, whereas this house, constituted as a committee of the whole in committee of supply, is in the main deliberative in its function. I think that is a very important function.
This has been a very useful debate. Even the hon. member for Burnaby-Seymour (Mr. Perrault) agrees because in his speech he said it had been a good debate and had proceeded in the best tradition of parliament. We have heard excellent cases put forward by those speaking from both sides on this extremely important and urgent matter of procedure. In the main I think that the views expressed have been responsible. I subscribe to that, as I am sure my colleagues do, 100 per cent.
With regard to responsibility, we have just seen how the house can take its responsibility seriously. This was demonstrated in a move whereby debate at the resolution stage of a very important bill was waived by unanimous consent of the house. Unanimous consent could not have been possible unless the house leaders were in agreement and hon. members were unanimous in respect of that agreement. We have just passed without debate the resolution stage of the important bill to amend the Criminal Code, the so-called omnibus bill, in order that members may have the bill before them to study over the Christmas recess, if indeed there is to be one, and hence make a more useful contribution to the deliberations on that important piece of legislation.
Similarly, last evening we had another example of the house taking its responsibility seriously when we agreed, again by consent and after consultation, to limit debate on the resolution preceding the bill to establish a freshwater fish marketing board. We agreed to limit our debate at the resolution stage with the knowledge that we were giving up an opportunity accorded to us whereby we could have debated at great length the very serious crisis facing the groundfish industry in the Atlantic provinces. As hon. members who were present in the house know, we limited ourselves to a debate of just under two hours, I believe. We completed the resolution stage and now have the bill so that when we reconvene we can get right into the legislation. Those who are interested in the bill, the governments of the prairie provinces and others, will have a chance to see the legislation and appreciate exactly what is entailed in it.
As I have said, Mr. Speaker, this is just another example of what can be accomplished by consultation, agreement, showing good will and being prepared to give a little in discussing the business of the house with the
December 19, 1968	COMMONS
various house leaders of the opposition parties. It is also well worth noting that this important debate on the rules was also adjourned by unanimous consent and after consultation and agreement among the house leaders of the opposition parties and the government house leader. Under our present rules it would not have been possible to adjourn the debate without this agreement. However, hon. members, taking their responsibility seriously as parliamentarians, agreed to forgo the rules whereby this debate would have had to be continued in order that Canada could fulfil an international obligation that the government had undertaken. We did that and considered the legislation dealing with anti-dumping duties. As I say, these are examples of what can be accomplished by agreement.
I have made a brief reference to the fishing industry and the very serious crisis facing that industry in Canada. Just a few weeks ago we were able, by our questions in the house, to get the government house leader to bring on the estimates of the Department of Fisheries. Using that as a vehicle, we were able to have an emergency debate on the very serious problems facing the fishery of the Atlantic provinces. I raise this point because without the committee of supply, without the means to at least be able to consider some of the estimates in the house, a very useful vehicle of debate would be done away with. As a consequence, members of this house who feel it necessary to bring to the attention of the house matters which they consider of great urgency or indeed which may be in the national interest and of great national urgency would not have this traditional opportunity to bring these matters up in the committee of supply during the traditional examination of estimates or in committee of the whole house.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
As I said at the outset of my remarks, this type of deliberation is not possible under our present committee system, and if the government has its way and these rules are adopted we will not have the opportunity now accorded to us to bring up, to debate and to make speeches on matters we consider to be of national urgency and in the national interest. As a private member of the house I consider this a matter of great regret because it is a traditional right under our British parliamentary system that members can bring up grievances before granting supply to Her Majesty. This is a traditional and long fought
DEBATES	4163
Motion for Concurrence in Report for right of parliament. It is most regrettable that we will lose this tradition and this right and that we will not, in my submission, have the same opportunities in the future, if these rules are adopted, to bring up matters of great importance, great urgency and great emergency.
If these rules are adopted in their present form it is my wish and the wish of many of the hon. members who have participated in this debate that some changes be made in our committee system to make the committees more meaningful, to make them forums which would lend themselves to more meaningful examination of estimates and provide the means whereby this examination can take place. We are now used to having to meet in very limited surroundings. Sometimes committees overlap and one finds oneself having to be in two places at once. We had an instance of this during the present session when I found myself greatly interested in the deliberations of the transport and communications committee, as indeed many members from the Atlantic provinces were. On a particular day that committee was considering the estimates of the National Harbours Board and coincidentally with that meeting the committee on regional development was considering the report of the Atlantic Development Board. I raised a point of order at that time requesting that the chairman of the regional development committee bring this to the attention of the co-ordinating committee to ensure that overlapping is avoided if possible, especially on committees of interest to the same members. It is a well known fact that hon. members from the Atlantic provinces and from the other maritime areas in Canada would be greatly interested in the report of the National Harbours Board and at the same time the same hon. members would be greatly interested in the report of the Atlantic Development Board. This is one of the great weaknesses in the present committee system. It is a matter of great regret if we adopt the rules in their present form and have to refer estimates to the standing committees as they are now constituted.
The hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Blair) said that debates on supply estimates tend to be general speech-making events and that most of the discussion takes place on the first item. I do not quarrel with that statement because this is a well known fact. All of the well known authorities on parliament have stated that debate generally tends to take place on the first item because
4164	COMMONS DEBATES	December 19, 1968
Motion for Concurrence in Report the rule of relevancy is not so strictly applied. Thus hon. members can make far-reaching speeches, examine all aspects of the department and in so doing present their case to the committee, but in order to present their case it is necessary for them to make speeches. I find myself in agreement with the hon. member and I find nothing wrong with this procedure. Again I repeat that if these rules are adopted we will not have the opportunity to present our case in the committees of the house.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FOURTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
We will be deprived of the opportunity to present arguments building toward the investigation or interrogation of the minister or of the various departments whose estimates we are considering. I looked up one of the noted authorities on parliament, Erskine May, and in his 17th edition at page 765 he says in essence that criticism of departmental administration which usually takes place on the first item is "the real business of supply", that is, the real business of the examination of the estimates. It is the traditional practice and right of parliamentarians before granting supply to present their grievances to the house and thereby to the government and to say: Yes, we will vote you the money but before doing so we will take the opportunity accorded to us under our rules and according to the custom of parliament to present our grievances to the government. As I said, this is neither practical nor possible in the standing committees as they are now constituted.
Speaking of the committees as they are now constituted, one has only to look to the committee on transport and communications. I will not say much about it because the subject matter has been referred by an order of the house to the standing committee on privileges and elections as the result of a question of privilege. But the fact remains that because of the partisan nature of committees and because of the partisanship of the chairmen of committees the committee on transport and communications in presenting its second report to this house deliberately, in my view, left out of its report a very important resolution legally passed and adopted by the committee. One can only conclude that that resolution was left out because it was not palatable to the government. Consequently, this points up the fact that unless our committee system is changed and unless members of the opposition are recognized as having 
their full rights and responsibilities in the committees as they have in the house in the examination of estimates and the granting of supply, the referring of all the estimates to the committees as they are now constituted is nothing but a farce.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FOURTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FOURTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
If the committees are given real powers, then perhaps a case can be made for a useful examination of estimates. But in saying that I would point out to the house that ours is not the congressional system. Thank God we still operate under the British parliamentary system. One must make that distinction. We do not have the enormous research facilities and the research help accorded to the committees of the United States congress. When we examine estimates in committee and interrogate witnesses in relation to those estimates we have to do the best we can as members of the house in presenting our questions knowing full well that the minister has behind him all the experts and all the substantial resources of the particular department that we happen to be investigating or whose estimates we are examining at the time. In contrast members of the U.S. congress and its committees have substantial resources assigned to them and moneys voted to them for this purpose by the House of Representatives. The committees of the United States congress do substantial work because the members of these committees are well equipped and have huge staffs to enable them to conduct useful interrogation and useful investigation.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I suggest to the government, Mr. Speaker, and those hon. members who speak so highly of depriving us of our traditional right of granting supply in a committee of the whole house and referring all estimates to committees, that they bear in mind the distinct difference between our British parliamentary system and the congressionnal system in the United States. In that regard I commend the useful, very sensible and very moderate suggestion by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) in opening this debate for our party, namely, that we retain at least 20 per cent of the estimates in the house and refer the remainder to committees. In that way we would still have a forum in which we could bring up matters of great urgency to the country.
In his criticism of the committee of supply the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said that
December 19. 1988	COMMONS
members did not seek information but rather made speeches. Well, what is wrong with making speeches? What is wrong with having useful debate in this house? The hon. member for Burnaby-Seymour spoke of the useful debate we are having now on these important rule changes. How else can we represent our constituencies? How else can we represent our provinces? How else can we usefully represent the country if we are not given the opportunity to present our views in this house?
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the Prime Minister is bored. He does not like speeches. Pie does not like parliament for that reason. He does not like deliberative speechmaking, which is the main reason for the existence of parliament. I say to the Prime Minister. That is too bad. I say to the Prime Minister also that the government which he heads is playing with weapons that are very dangerous to the future of the country. When they start fooling around with the traditional, long fought for rights of parliament, when members are not allowed to make speeches to bring up grievances before granting supply, then they are playing with dangerous weapons. Let the Prime Minister come out and say he wants to amend the constitution and have a congressional system. Why does he not have the courage to say that instead of taking from us our rights in this house on a piecemeal basis and doing away with the very symbols of our British parliamentary system? In my view, if he has his way parliament as we know it will cease to exist and that will be a dark day for this country.
I see the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. MacEachen) in the house. I hope he is going to participate in this debate because he was one of the most successful house leaders the government has had. I think it is a matter of regret that the hon. gentleman is not still the house leader because we would not have the problems we have today. I say that with great deference to the hon. and sometimes humble President of the Privy Council. The great problem is that he does not seem to be able to trust the other house leaders, and this is why he finds himself in trouble today.

Motion for Concurrence in Report I believe, as do other hon. members who have participated in this debate, that our rules have to be modified; they have to be reformed. Nobody will quarrel with that statement. Our rules have to be reformed from time to time and brought up to date to make sure that our institution of parliament relates to the needs of the day. Yet I say we should not tinker with the basic rights of members of the house. Generally speaking, I think the proposed changes, especially those in 16-A and the proposal to take all the estimates out of the committee of supply, go far beyond the necessary reforms needed to bring parliament up to date and make it relate to the present day.
In my view, Mr. Speaker, when you take away from this house its deliberative function, when you take away from this house the right of private members to stand up and bring their grievances before the government, you weaken this institution to the point where it will some day disappear before our eyes. When that happens we will probably have government by directive. Let us abolish parliament altogether. Why bother going through first and second readings of bills, the committee stage, and so on? Why not do away with parliament entirely if the Prime Minister does not like it? He has a majority.
Why does the Prime Minister not come out and say: I have no use for this institution, so let us abolish it and have government by directive? This is the kind of government there is in the Soviet countries, in countries where there are dictatorships of either the extreme right or left. This is what we had in my own province of Newfoundland. We had government by directive when our constitution was suspended in 1933. We had a dictatorship imposed upon us by Britain. Our people had no say. We had government by directive, and as a consequence of that we came into confederation 50 years behind the other maritime provinces. This was the result of not having a parliament. Our people had no voice in the affairs of our province. I feel very strongly on this subject because I grew up in Newfoundland not knowing what the institution of parliament was. My people had no vote and they had no parliament to represent them. They had no place to present their grievances except by direct petition to the Queen at Westminster. Now this government is tinkering with the very thing of which we were deprived, our right to stand in this house and present our grievances to the government before granting supply.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member who has just taken his seat for introducing me to the house, and I gladly accept his invitation to participate in this very important debate. I had the honour of being a member of the committee which presented this report during part of its deliberations, and in the last parliament of Canada I had the honour of being the chairman of the special committee that presented a number of reports to parliament, the recommendations contained in which have been incorporated in part in this report that we have been debating. I want to congratulate the members of the committee, especially the chairman, the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Blair) for the leadership that he gave the committee, for producing the reports under the rather stringent time schedule that we all wanted to have.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
Personally, I believe that the changes that will be made in the rules as a result of the adoption of these reports will strengthen the House of Commons and make the institution more meaningful to the Canadian people. It is because of that view that I support the major conclusions of the report. Indeed, they will make the Canadian House of Commons more British. If the hon. member who has just taken his seat thanks God, as he did, for

living under the British parliamentary system, then he ought to encourage his group to do in the Canadian parliament the things that have been done in the British parliament to make it more effective and meaningful.
I was a member of a committee that visited Westminster and conferred with a number of British leaders. The government house leader, Right Hon. Richard Crossman, told us bluntly that we were living under 19th century rules of procedure. He said to us: "You are way back where we were in the last century". Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to take up the time of the house for very long in saying one or two things about this debate. I am going to support the adoption of the committee's report that is before the house at the present time. May I say I have been very impressed by the tenor and high quality of the debate in the house this afternoon, particularly the magnificent speech by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. MacEachen). I hope that the offer he made to end the present impasse will be accepted, that the proposed rule 16A will be held in abeyance pending further study and the rest of the proposals made by the committee will be accepted and approved by the House of Commons.
A great deal has been said about the inherent danger involved in adopting the committee's report. It is said that this would present a danger to our democratic process. However, it occurs to me that a greater danger lies in failing to agree to a timetable prepared by the house leaders of the different parties, and certainly there is a danger of our leaders failing to agree to such a timetable among themselves.
Timetables for debate and for the length of such debates on government legislation presented to the house have been used by most modern democratic parliamentary institutions. This is particularly true, as has been pointed out this afternoon, in the House of Commons in the United Kingdom, where such a timetable has been in operation for many years

under both Labour and Conservative administrations. There is no doubt that the development of parliamentary government is a subject of contention and controversy. Just the same, parliamentarians feel that there is need for talk on every subject that comes up for consideration. However, shortage of time does not permit us to talk for long, much less to obstruct and far less to filibuster.
Democracy cannot survive in face of obstructionist tactics on the part of elected oppositions in democratic parliaments. I am not saying that such a thing takes place in this chamber, certainly not by design or by contrivance. I have too many friends on both sides of the house to level any such accusation. Nevertheless, the danger of obstructionist, defeatist and filibustering tactics could be fatal to the democratic process in modern times, just as fatal in Canada as it could be in the United Kingdom. Is this country going to be compared with Russia, China and other countries that have no orderly democratic parliamentary practices? Good government is necessary for any nation to succeed in the world today.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
We must sacrifice some of the inherited rules of practice and procedure in this House of Commons. This is not easy for us. Most of us I think want to maintain the old, traditional rules of the parliament of Canada. But in the modem world of technology I say that parliamentary reform is absolutely essential if we are not to be bypassed and if parliamentary government is to be effective. Here in Canada each of us should be thankful that we can express our views on matters of national importance. But we must be brief, we must be disciplined, and we must not overplay our individual rights and the liberty we have as members of parliament to oppose and to criticize. I fail to see why the present impasse should not be broken. In my opinion, what is asked by the President of the Privy Council is not so unreasonable. Can the opposition parties not agree to a time limit on bills that are to come before the house?

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. S-ll, to incorporate Aetna Casualty Company of Canada.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill seeks the incorporation of a company under the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act to carry on business in all classes of insurance other than life insurance. A similar bill has been introduced in previous sessions and I believe that many hon. members who are here are familiar with it. For this reason I shall keep my opening comments brief but will be happy to answer any questions that there may be with regard to the details of the bill.
The proposed company would be a subsidiary of the Aetna Casualty and Surety Insurance Company of Hartford, Connecticut. This is a respectable company which already carries on business with its affiliate, the Standard Fire Insurance Company, in all the classes of insurance for which application is being made in this bill to incorporate the new Canadian company. In brief, therefore, what this bill seeks to do is to permit this respectable and reputable group to carry on business through a Canadian incorporation rather than through the United States parent company and its affiliate.
The parent company, the Aetna Casualty Company of Hartford, has held a certificate of registry under the Foreign Insurance Companies Act of Canada for the past 49 years. It has reviewed its operations in Canada and has concluded it would be desirable for the Canadian business to be carried on by a company incorporated in Canada. That, in brief, is the object and purposes of this bill.
I think hon. members will be interested in how the company proposes to operate in Canada. Pending the establishment of the Canadian company, in order to expand its operations in Canada the parent company in September, 1966, opened an office in Toronto which is known as the head office for Canada. It is headed by a Canadian who is general manager for Canada. Canadians are also selected to head the fidelity and surety and underwriting operations for this office.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
There are presently 97 employees in this office, 71 of whom are Canadians. Of the 26 non-Canadian employees in Toronto, only 10 are United States citizens. Of the five non-Canadians in Montreal three are United

December 19, 1968

States citizens and of the four non-Canadians in other offices one is a United States citizen. In September 1968, an office was opened in Montreal. The head of the Toronto office is responsible for the operations of this office which numbers 41 Canadians among its 46 employees. All present employees of these two offices would become employees of the Canadian company. The parent company now has claim offices located in Quebec City, Ottawa, Hamilton, Winnipeg, Calgary and Vancouver. All but four of the 50 present employees in the six claim offices are Canadians and all present employees would become employees of the Canadian company.
In the two years since the Toronto office opened in September 1966, the number of employees in Canadian operations has increased from 90 to 193. Normal growth would indicate that by the end of five years employees in Canadian operations would number 450 of which at least 90 per cent would be Canadians. The Canadian company would be under the direction of the general manager for Canada who would have charge of the company's operations throughout Canada. Underwriting, sales, engineering and accounting will continue to be centralized in the head office at Toronto but, as the need becomes evident, facilities for these services will be placed in other important cities in Canada, as occurred with the opening of the Montreal office in September, 1968. Of course the experience and services of the United States company will be available for the assistance of the Canadian company.
One might ask what objection there could be to the incorporation of this company. I think perhaps the objection that would be raised is that it is intended to be a subsidiary of a United States company and that its capital will be United States capital.

Yet there is no law against the incorporation of Canadian companies which are subsidiaries of United States companies. This house would have the option to pass such a law if it chose. Until such a law is passed it seems to me that these companies should be treated on the same basis as other companies and that if they are prepared to abide by our laws their incorporation should be welcomed. Capital from the United States should continue to be welcomed in Canada as long as the owners of that capital abide by our regulations and conduct themselves as good corporate citizens of Canada.

This company if incorporated will be subject to regulation by our Department of Insurance. The form of the bill of incorporation is standard. I understand there is no objection from the Department of Insurance to the incorporation of this company. I believe that probably all members of the house will agree that increased competition in the general insurance business in Canada would be an excellent thing from the point of view of the ordinary Canadian who from time to time buys insurance. This is a reputable company. The formation of a subsidiary in Canada will assist in extending its business and increasing competition in this important field and will confer positive advantages upon Canadians.
Members may be interested in the record of the company with regard to profits made in Canadian business. I have been informed it is the intention of the company to leave any underwriting profits in Canada in order to strengthen the financial structure of the Canadian company. With regard to the personnel policy I have been informed that a primary objective of the company will continue to be to employ Canadians in the management of the operation to the extent they are available. Of course nearly all clerical personnel will be Canadians.
In brief the establishment of the company or its incorporation as a Canadian company will create for Canada additional employment and additional capital funds. Additional capital is something which we need a great deal of in Canada at the present time. The parent company has stated that it looks upon the establishment of the company as an additional thrust for the already demonstrated expanding Canadian economy and as a permanent and growing part of this economy.
If there are any questions with regard to the company I will be happy to do my best to answer them. I hope it may be possible this afternoon to refer the bill to the appropriate committee where a more detailed study of the company and the proposed place of this company in Canada can be considered.

Mr. Speaker, we certainly welcome and listened with interest to the introductory remarks of the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Wahn) with regard to this bill. I think, however, with all respect and not unkindly, that there is a certain misleading element in the hon. member's remarks. This does not detract from his sincerity in presenting them, but I think there is another side of the picture which should be disclosed. I have in mind the question of a

foreign owned company meeting no objection by the Department of Insurance.
If I might be permitted to deal very briefly with the ideas expressed by the hon. gentleman, I should like to indicate to the house in what respect I do not think they are in the full sense valid reasons for accepting the proposition that we should endorse the bill. I understood the hon. member to say that foreign capital should be welcome in Canada as long as the owners of that capital obey our laws, regulations and the like. I do not even know whether the reference to obeying the law is necessary. The purpose of having laws is that they be obeyed. I would not even presume to cast any reflection on the company by suggesting it had any other intention than to obey the laws and regulations and work within them.
The assertion that foreign capital should be welcomed if the owners of that capital obey the laws of the country really begs the question of whether or not we should continue the practice of endorsing foreign capital investments in Canada to the extent that they control sections of our economy. That is the question that we should be dealing with and not whether or not they will obey the law. There is no presumption on my part or, I am sure, on the part of other hon. members that the Aetna company has any other thought than to live by our laws and regulations.
With regard to no objections having been made by the Department of Insurance, in terms of foreign control this is meaningless because Mr. Humphrys, the Superintendent of Insurance can do nothing else but simply look at the bill and the structure of the company in the light of the law as set out in the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act. Mr. Humphrys has no authority to look at the matter of foreign ownership with regard to whether it is good, bad, or otherwise. Simply to say that the bill should be passed because the Superintendent of Insurance has given it his stamp of approval is not really a valid argument for passing the bill. Mr. Humphrys is a public servant and, like many other people in the Public Service of Canada, assiduous as he is he simply follows the narrow letter of the law which guides him. He has no authorization to step outside those bounds.
In fact, I am rather surprised that Mr. Humphrys permits himself to be used as an advocate of some kind in respect of some of these companies when he appears before the committee. In many cases, and this one is no

exception, Mr. Humphrys would appear to be the advocate of the company itself because he is the one who presents all the reasons and provides all the answers and explanations in respect of how the company intends to operate and what it intends to do, while the officers of the company who appear before the committee often say relatively little. This, I think, is a pity. The officers and lawyers representing these companies sit in the background and let Mr. Humphrys, the Superintendent of Insurance, carry the ball for them in presenting the case.

I also hope that members of the committee will confine their questions to this simple relationship, and that the officers of these companies will reply to questions concerning the directors and so on and not leave Mr. Humphrys, the Superintendent of Insurance, to carry the ball for them.
This bill was considered by the banking and commerce committee of the Senate on October 23 of this year. Mr. Humphrys was there, together with officers representing Aetna, and certain questions were asked about a subject which in my view is the fundamental aspect with which we should be concerned here, namely, the degree of foreign ownership involved.
As an aside, perhaps I can say that once again evidence was given relating to the number of people working in the different offices of the company, the number who were Canadians and the number who were not Canadians. But this information is not material to the point I have in mind. It does not really matter whether 100 per cent of the employees in the company's Canadian operation are Canadian citizens. It is still someone in Hartford, Connecticut, who is calling the shots and making the decisions. Even if all the people in the Canadian offices were born and raised in Canada, even if they

Mr. Speaker, I know the house would agree to extend the time of the hon. member, if he asked, but we would not want to deprive other members of the opportunity to take part in this lively debate. The Aetna Casualty Company is an old friend; they have been before us at least three times. On each occasion we have been opposed to the incorporation in Canada of a foreign owned company. This company is operating in Canada and has been for many years. We have no particular objection to that, and there is nothing we could do about it if we did have an objection. We are objecting to their coming into Canada and establishing a subsidiary company to operate like a Canadian company on the Canadian scene, without giving that Canadian company the autonomy that would in fact make it, as a former minister of trade and commerce used to say, a good Canadian corporate citizen. This company obviously does not intend to be a good corporate citizen at all.
In fact, when questions were asked on this matter the answer was that the insurance business is an international matter and therefore should not recognize the bounds of nationalism, or any other provincial or state restriction that would limit it. This sounds very much like the Rothschilds when they talk about finance. They believe that money has no conscience, no nationality and no patriotism, and therefore it does not have to be a good corporate citizen. Their theory is

that you can take money where you can get it; there is no dirty money, no matter from what source it comes. They believe that money from the common brothel is as good as that which comes from somebody's hard earned pay cheque.
I believe this is something with which many Canadians will disagree. I disagree with it, as I am sure do many of my colleagues. I think many members of the house agree that we face in this company a phenomenon that has taken place on the North American continent in the last 50 years and in fact has spread to all countries of the world. We face a totally different type of company than that which was originally formed when the great American interest developed, in the mercantile sense, when the United States was able to gain the benefit of money from other countries without losing their soul in the process.
When the United States was starting as an industrial nation and needed large amounts of capital-and there is certainly a similarity between their progress 100 years ago and ours today-they were able to borrow these sums of money in the form of direct loans. This money was paid back, together with the interest charged in respect of it. Companies were originated because of the capital obtained and the generation of input from other sources, namely Dutch and British interests, and the people who lent the money got it back, plus the interest. But when it was all over it was apparent that the economy in that area was more vibrant and self-sustaining. As it happened they went bankrupt.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
This is not what is happening in Canada in this case. Here is a company that has a very large interest in the United States. There is no question about its being an old and reliable insurance company which has been doing business in Canada for years and which has been supervised to a certain extent by Canadian authorities in terms of the liabilities it retains. However, in the main it has been operating as a corporate citizen, not even of the United States but of a state in the United States, because of some insurance principle that must have existed in Connecticut which was not common to other states. I think that any hon. member interested in background information relating to insurance companies could look up the insurance legislation of the state of Connecticut and he would find that hundreds of insurance companies have their
December 19. 1968

head offices in Hartford, Connecticut because the legislation in that state is favourable to their business.
There is no reason why we as Canadians being faced, with the development of a new company which desires to do business in this country, and to operate under our protection and our legislation, should not demand that they set up a Canadian corporate company. That is not what is being done. This will never be a Canadian company but only a federally incorporated company. It will be supervised by our superintendent of insurance but it will always be a foreign owned and foreign dominated company because it is only a subsidiary. This has been the history of insurance companies in Canada. I have already said that the United States was able to develop on borrowed capital; we have been able to develop as an extension with subsidiary companies in every industry in Canada, as a consequence of which we do not own any of the industrial development of this nation and we continue to operate only with branch offices. I suppose the easy way out for the company would be to buy government securities, but it will be necessary for them to carry in Canada only the amount of money needed to cover their liabilities, and I doubt if the company will maintain much capital beyond that.
It surprises me that members of parliament, who are surely as good Canadians as I hope I am, fail to see the dangers that are entailed in allowing these very capable companies to come into Canada and operate in such a manner that they can never become part of the Canadian development. I think it is important for us to be aware of our potentialities. This company wants to come to Canada and do business here. I am sure that if we had a law specifying that all the directors on the board of the company must be Canadians, and that a certain percentage of their shares must be owned by Canadians, the situation would be different. All the companies that want to start operating in Canada want to have a big investment on their money. So long as this is the case and so long as they get a reasonable interest, they will want to remain on the Canadian scene. On the other hand, we as Canadians should insist on the right to buy into those companies and to become part owners. If tomorrow we were to pass a law saying that 75 per cent of this company must be Canadian owned, they 29180-2651

would surely be willing to set up their company here and to sell their stock on the market in the hope that Canadians would pick it up. Obviously $500,000 is a small amount of money for this company to pay to cover their incorporation. They really could do much better than this if they wanted to, but that is all we require and that is what they will provide to obtain their incorporation.

I suggest that what I have said is supported by a number of members of the house. We have had requests from several insurance companies recently to establish companies in Canada. I was very pleased to talk to one of the presidents of one of these insurance companies who indicated that for a long time he has been a dummy director of a U.S. subsidiary but that he, as an intelligent Canadian with a considerable amount of money, had no desire to be a dummy director of a U.S. corporation. If it wishes to operate in Canada, as it has been doing for a number of years, then I am prepared to let it do so. I am not suggesting that the Aetna Insurance Company is a particularly good or a particularly bad company. I am just saying that it should not be given the rights and advantages of a Canadian citizen in the corporate world, without any of the responsibilities.
We give Mr. Humphrys, the superintendent of insurance, a great deal of responsibility to carry out on our behalf. I am surprised to note how many of the Senators, who have a great interest in insurance companies because they are on the board of directors of many of them, look to Mr. Humphrys for advice on whether or not to underwrite other companies. Mr. Humphrys is bound by the regulations we make or by the lack of them.
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
One of the things that really surprised me not long ago when dealing with an insurance company was that the company had agreed that within ten years they would have 51 per cent of the ownership of the company in the hands of Canadians. As a matter of fact, if they did not, they would be out of business. When they went to Mr. Humphrys they found that because of a regulation passed by this house, for reasons of which I am not aware, it was impossible for us to write a clause into this bill providing for 51 per cent control in the hands of Canadians. If the company were to get 51 per cent of their stock in the hands of Canadians, it would only be able to vote 10 per cent of its stock. I do not know how the officials arrive at this decision. There are only one or two people here today, and I suppose one would be the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson), who would know about this. The provision has some relationship to negotiations with the Mercantile Bank at the time the banking legislation was being considered. I do not know why 51 per cent of the shares in the hands of Canadians would leave the company in the position of being able to vote only 10 per cent of the stock. Mr. Humphrys advised that only 49 per cent of the controlling shares can be divested from the parent company, or the company will technically lose control and only be able to vote 10 per cent of the stock.
The company was not prepared to do that, and I don't blame them. I really do not understand why this type of restriction is

involved in this matter. As I say, I did not have the opportunity of being a member of the banking and commerce committee, so I am unfamiliar with the reasoning behind this legislation. I suggest that some members of our banking and commerce committee or some members who are here tonight who are interested in this matter should give some consideration to the reason for this regulation. It certainly surprised the corporation lawyer from the United States who looked into the matter. He could not understand why we would do this, and he was familiar with the regulations in many other countries. He pointed out to us that countries like Japan insisted on de facto ownership in the hands of nationals. This provision probably goes much further than the one we are suggesting.

I believe the present government is trying to be a good successor to great Canadian governments of the past, as well as to make us the heirs of this great British tradition of parliamentary government that has existed for many generations and which has been furthered by men like Gladstone and others of historical importance, and perfected in recent times.

I am proud of our traditions, but I know-and I think we all know- that they should be improved, and improved greatly, in order to effect the proper dispatch of business before the House of Commons, and to make it more readily possible for parliament to meet the issues of the day and the challenges of our times. Failure to have a timetable for debate, and to tailor our debating time will set us all on a hopeless path, allowing for inadequate and second rate leadership for the Canadian people and for this country in the modern competitive world of today.
There are many in this house who fear that the government will misuse its power if this report is adopted. However, I want to say with great sincerity that in a democratic country there is just as much fear that an opposition composed of several parties will misuse its power as there is that the government will be guilty of a similar misuse. Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the words of the hon. member for Brant, one of the more serious and sincere members of this house, and in many ways I agree with the sentiments he expressed in his eulogistic closing remarks. When he says that time is on the side of the future may I point out that this institution has been here longer than any of us have been alive, and it will continue in some form long after we have departed.
This debate is not being continued for the sake of stirring up the polls. We are not trying to stir up the public merely because it is Christmastime, and because we think it ought to be interested in the procedural debate. Frankly I do not think that Canadians are terribly interested in this debate because I do not think they appreciate fully the significance of the main points being debated.
[Mr. Brown.1
This afternoon the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. MacEachen) entered the debate, and his contribution certainly was entertaining and energetically delivered, even if his remarks had partisan political overtones. But I was surprised to see him buy the package so soon. After all, the wrapping is not off it. This afternoon we heard from the government side a qualified proposal with regard to the point we are debating. As one who always believed in what is commonly referred to as participatory politics, I wondered what the proposal meant. I know that the house leaders discussed certain matters, such as the Christmas recess, and that we are to come back on January 14. Other than that, before the Minister of Manpower and Immigration had made his remarks this afternoon, I was under the impression that there had been no consultation, without prejudice, about any proposal.
I only hope my hon. friend from Brant does not have too many children. I have a few and I can tell him that my children like to look under the tinsel of the wrapping to see what gifts there are under the tree. They get excited and they like to remove the tinsel. It is true that television has great persuasive powers, and that advertising can sway the opinion of many. However, that does not detract from my suggestion that much of what we have seen represents tinsel, and we do not really know what the underlying package is. In many ways the government is treating us like children waiting for Santa Claus, only they will not take off the tinsel from the gifts under the tree. We want to see what is under the tinsel, what is in the package. No doubt the hon. member for Brant was speaking with the approval of the cabinet. He made many fine statements; all the same we don't know what sort of present the government has for us since all we have seen, basically, is tinsel. That is the problem.
Although the Minister of Manpower and Immigration was most entertaining, it seemed to me that his participation was somewhat artificial. Without doubt the government received a mandate on June 25 to govern this country. It has the right to govern, even though the opposition parties may not like it. The government has its responsibilities to fulfil, and it ought to know, as it no doubt does, that tonight it has the power to cut off any debate in this house, after giving 24 hours notice that it wishes to impose the guillotine.
There was no need for the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) to lecture the house
December 19, 1968

about the right of the government to govern; we accept that. Parties on both sides of the house have used the guillotine procedure. Governments of other, historical periods have used it. The question here is not whether the guillotine ought to be used, but the circumstances under which it may be used: That is the issue. There is no question here of the majority in the house being pitted against the minority. The basic question here is whether parliament shall be an effective instrument of the people, or merely efficient. I suggest respectfully that the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Manpower and Immigration in this debate have committed a form of parliamentary perjury in trying to build a man of straw. We know that on this side of the house we are in a minority, although I hasten to add that the opposition side obtained the votes of 54 per cent of the Canadian people.
I deplore the technique of the big lie and I suggest, seriously, that if politics is in disrepute tonight it is because men who ought to know better have perverted their principles for the sake of power. That is what I mean when I speak of parliamentary perjury.
I notice that an hon. member of the rump seems agitated. I suggest that if he wishes to participate in this debate, he should do so or he will discover that the government house leader has allocated his time. Unless an hon. member sits on the treasury benches he will have hardly any opportunity to speak.
Just consider that, Mr. Speaker. This debate began on Tuesday, December 10, and has continued for six days. Since the contribution of the hon. member for Burnaby-Seymour (Mr. Perrault), ten members from the government side have spoken. I think about 12 altogether have spoken from the government side, and I think I am the thirteenth speaker to talk on behalf of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition. Some hon. member says that is too many, but this is an issue which affects the fundamental framework of this chamber and a mere 12 members out of the 150, odd, opposite have participated. I think that some other intelligent members on that side would like to contribute to the debate. I would suggest that unless some of them come forward in the next day or two and speak, then there has already been an allocation of time in this debate so far as the government is concerned.

Being a backbencher, I think backbenchers should have a real interest in what this debate is all about. Yet only 12 members

As yet the government house leader has not answered the question I asked him several nights ago. I asked, on his figuring of 80 days left in this session, how many days he was prepared to allot in advance for the debate on the Criminal Code bill.
This debate is not over the right of the government to govern and bring in closure when it feels there is obstruction. The whole purpose of this debate has not been as suggested by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in his opening remarks, that there is a time for debate and a time for decision. The paradox, the irony is that this government, which has been so instrumental in trying to cut off every traditional concept that we have had in this country for 100 odd years, is now trying to rationalize its position by relying holus-bolus on the British system. Forgetting about the judicial principle that you cannot quote a case unless it is on all fours with the case at bar, the case the minister used was completely irrelevant to the issue in this debate. bill other than once, other than the example given by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration, when it was used on two bills that were related and had come through the whole process back to back. That is why the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) and other members on this side can stand up and say that, so far as 16-A is concerned, it is completely unheard of in practical form and effect in any democratic parliament anywhere in the world.
It is an interesting commentary on this whole debate that, after all the dust of battle had settled, after the Minister of Manpower and Immigration had castigated some of the members in the opposition and supported the British system so completely, what does he come up with? He comes up with a proposal. I sincerely suggest that this should have been discussed beforehand with the house leaders, as are most proposals, but for the first time he advanced it on the floor of this chamber.
When a man from the treasury benches can stand up in this place, after six days of debate, and advance a proposal of change from a rigid, firm, inflexible position, that is the justification for our being against 16-A. That proposal did not come after a time limit had been imposed by hon. members opposite. It came after the free flow of debate, after some of the public got interested, after some of the papers became interested, and after a lot of hon. members became interested. I venture to say that when this debate started a majority of the government members did not understand the effect and implications of 16-A. By making that proposal this afternoon the minister justified this forum. The reason for this forum is to have suggestions and counter suggestions, proposals and counter proposals made on the floor of the house, open to the scrutiny of the public, so that a consensus can build.
We on this side want a consensus after debate. We don't want a computer before the debate even begins.
So far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, it is 16-A which sticks in the throat of any parliamentarian. It must stick in the throat of any parliamentarian, if he is worth his salt, because no parliamentarian in the world has accepted it.

If we take the British system and look at all the procedure points, so called, which they have, we should ask whether they have more or less problems today; is their parliamentary status and the status of the parliamentarians there any higher than it is in this country. I venture to say it is not.
I could philosophize. They are supposed to have a very modern efficient system. I suggest the state of parliament, in Britain, let alone the state of the member of parliament, is no higher than some people think it is here, because they have problems which will not be resolved by some of the procedures here. This is a form of parliamentary perjury which puts many things under suspicion, when better men know better what they are talking about.
This is a package of reform which some people feel may deform parliament. We might not agree with it, but it is there; it is a package of reform. I do not know whether the government has been playing a game of Russian roulette in trying to advance to the extreme, so that they can retreat to a more constructive position. We on this side of the house are as com-plately dedicated to reform as is any member of the opposition. But we are not for reaction. I suggest in all seriousness that 16A, coming from a Liberal government that calls itself liberal, is the most reactionary proposal advanced by any party in any country anywhere. It is pure reaction. We are for rules, but we are not for rulers. I am afraid, and my colleagues share my belief, that whether he likes it or not, 16A makes a ruler of the government house leader. Has he ever been on a plane that went from Signal Hill in Newfoundland to Esquimalt; has he ever boarded a plane, travelled from coast to coast in a day and seen all the regions of the country; or has any government leader seen this country, the regions and its people? It is preposterous to think that any one man, before the debate on a bill even begins, should be authorized to stand in his place and say that the debate will be limited to two days or five days.
Rule 16-A is unnecessary with a majority government. The problems we have in this parliament could not all have arisen since June 25. There is a backlog of business because there have been elections and because we have had minority parliaments. In addition there have been many promises which have not been kept. But does any member of this house who has read the rule expect that 16-A will help a minority government? Is any government house leader going to stand in his place and tell us that in the twenty seventh parliament he would have moved an order restricting debate before it began? If so, I suggest that by doing so he would have committed parliamentary suicide for himself or his party.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, it is unnecessary with a majority government. It does not help a minority government. It is unnecessary with a majority government because with the closure procedure they can cut off any debate in 24 hours. I suggest that this rule is unjust and makes a mockery of the just society. What is the whole reason for the much proclaimed Bill of Rights? It is to protect the rights of minorities against majorities that sometimes might be off the beat.
I do not question the sincerity of the Prime Minister in his life-long interest in a bill of rights. But I do wish he would stop preaching the platitudes of the Bill of Rights, and at the same time practise the type of parliamentary reform we have here tonight.
With all respect to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration I suggest, as I said earlier, that in practice 16-A is completely
December 19, 1968

Motion for Concurrence in Report unheard of in any parliamentary form of government in the British system. The unfortunate thing about this is that hon. members opposite do not seem to understand the scar tissue that is left by a debate which affects the rules of the house. There cannot be a debate, be it a pipe line debate, a defence production debate or any debate in which the combined opposition says no, without wounds being opened up.
Here we are in the 28th parliament with a government, which has a popular mandate, coming in at the first session and asking parliament for a rule which does not have the necessary experience behind it. I have only to look across at the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) and think back to a most interesting speech he gave in the House of Commons as recorded at page 1544 of Hansard in the year 1965. I know the minister remembers his speech better than I, because he gave it. I listened to the minister when he gave his speech in this debate on 16-A and the interesting thing is that he failed to point out what he said in respect of 15-A. Rule 15-A which has been in the rule books up until now, is not anywhere near as disastrous or as all-embracing as 16-A. What did he say about that? I am also greatly disturbed by paragraph 5 of the proposed standing order 15-A which provides as follows-
He then reads 15-A and gives very cogent reasons why we should be on guard about 15-A. Now he has changed his place, but I do not honestly believe his knowledge or policy has changed just because he changed his seat.
