The members of this house are in favour of reform, but they are not in favour of regimentation. This proposal will result only in more speed. We have all seen the speed with which events are dealt with by the television cameras just outside. I personally think they should be placed inside the chamber so that our debates are not redundant. It is getting so bad that those who sit on the treasury benches are wearing blue shirts, so that every time they make a statement they can look good outside. Television in this chamber would make debates relevant, not redundant, as so many of them are today. There is a difference between stability in legislation and sterility of legislation; there is a difference between making effective use of the talents of new members and this new rule in the name of so-called efficiency.
There is one expert who has not yet been quoted, a former member of this house who has had a great deal of experience with the rules. I refer to a lady called Pauline Jewett who wrote much on the subject of our rules, and I would refer now to a statement she made about the reform of parliament in the Journal of Canadian Studies for November, 1966. This makes the quotations used by the hon. member for Burnaby-Seymour (Mr. Per-rault) seem somewhat archiac, no matter how interesting the statements by my right hon. friend from Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker).

She admits that since the 27th parliament there has been a fundamental change. The limitation of time spent on estimates, the shortening of the question period, the abolition of the dinner period, the abolition from appeals from rulings by Mr. Speaker, the provision of one hour's notice to be given on certain questions of privilege, have all led to the more effective conduct of business. So, contrary to all one reads, the situation has changed a great deal in the last three or four years. We tend to forget this. Miss Jewett writes to the effect that there have been substantial changes in procedure, but that the government has failed to improve opportunities for new members to prepare for debates and take part in them. She says, on page 13:
At any rate, so rapidly was legislation processed in the first session of the 27th parliament that the cabinet was occasionally hard-pressed to keep the flow of bills, particularly of major bills like medicare, going forward. The most urgently needed reform now may well be the reorganization of departmental and cabinet machinery to secure greater efficiency in the preparation of government bills.
She goes on to suggest there should be someone in the Prime Minister's office whose job it would be to make sure that a regular flow of bills was being maintained. These are the view of a writer who is no friend of this side of the house but who is an acknowledged political scientist of considerable experience.
Looking across this chamber, I see the Minister of Manpower and Immigration. I have listened to the protests he has made so often about the right of collective bargaining. We have all heard him say that you cannot interfere with that process. Does he suggest that 16-A gives an opportunity for collective bargaining? Does he believe it gives adequate time for debate? Behind him on the benches opposite I see many hon. members who have been mayors of cities, chairmen of school boards, and so on. Do they believe that the introduction of 16-A to the proceedings of a city or town council, or of a school board, would improve the deliberations of such a council or board? I do not doubt that a good many mayors, a good many chairmen of school boards, might like to have such a rule, but before they agree to it I would be surprised if the members of the council or board did not slice their throats.
If the hon. member for Trois Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain) wishes to make a speech, he can do so at any time.
During the election campaign hon. gentlemen opposite made a special pitch for the involvement of youth in our affairs. They are

Is there any one of the younger members opposite who flocked to the banners of the flower people on June 25, who would take a seat in a university senate or on a board of governors and acquiesce when the president of the university or the chairman of the board of governors came in with an agenda which allowed for 20 minutes discussion of one subject, three minutes discussion of another and ten minutes discussion of a third? Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to see the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. MacEachen) back in the house. I was a little surprised to hear him say that the opposition-I think he was looking at the Conservatives but he probably included us as well- had little intellectual support or foundation for their arguments against proposed rule I6-A. The minister then proceeded to speak for at least 40 minutes, and it was probably closer to an hour, expounding what I regard as a rather illogical and anti-intellectual justification of his own position.
If I understood his arguments correctly, he was saying, "Look what has happened in the British Isles. Ergo: It should happen here." It seems to me that the most elementary class that one could take in the field of logic would teach you that this is a rather fallacious argument. If the principle under discussion is the practice of democracy, and you point to another parliamentary tradition and suggest that there has been a movement toward the centralization of authority and power in the system, it seems to me that you are not in a valid position to conclude from that that we should go on in the same way. One must argue, on independent grounds, for an authoritarian structure within a democratic society, if that is what you believe in-which of course, I do not. So I was not in the least bit persuaded by the arguments put forward by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration. It takes much more to be convinced of the desirability of a system than to have it demonstrated that this is done elsewhere and to be told "It is there, fellows; you must follow suit". If you want to have that kind of structure, it has to be argued for on quite independent grounds, and this I suggest the minister did not do.

Motion for Concurrence in Report [DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
I should like now to pursue what I think is the central issue in this debate, and that is the problem of democratic decision making. It seems to me it is very useful to look at a purported democratic society in terms of two categories. Its governmental institutions and its private or non-governmental institutions should be assessed in terms of the degree of democracy by providing answers to the three following questions: First, does the majority have decision-making power directly, or indirectly by controlling those who do; second, are decisions reached on the basis of a method involving ample and open discussion about differing proposals or conflicting goals; third, are minorities allowed to exist on a continuing basis which will enable them to have the potential of converting their minority position into a majority one?
I suggest that a society and its institutions can be assessed to be more or less democratic according to how well they meet these three criteria. Therefore, in our debate on the desirability of the proposed new rules for this house we should keep this in mind. It is worth noting at this time that efficiency is not an essential characteristic of a democratic society. Such societies or institutions may or may not be efficient. Whatever the case may be, the degree of efficiency does not affect our judgment concerning the degree of democracy characterizing an organization, institution or society. It has been argued sometimes that democratic institutions are likely to be more efficient. The contrary, of course, has also been argued, and perhaps even more frequently. My point is that efficiency, although at times worthy of being desired and pursued, has no essential or even important connection with the practice of democracy.
Efficiency, or rather a person's commitment to it, can, however, affect a democratic institution. Generally speaking, the more deeply a person or institution becomes committed to efficient action, the less likely will that person or institution be committed to democracy, more particularly to the means of democratic decision making. Expressed in another way, the man or institution more deeply committed to efficiency is also likely to be more prone to favour the concentration of power. If that man or institution also regards himself as being democratic, he is likely to confuse democracy with efficiency and is likely to be unaware that it is power, not democracy, that he is pursuing. If he abandons democratic
December 19, 1968

Motion for Concurrence in Report practices, he is also likely to do so in the name of democracy.
I suggest that this is what the minister was indulging in this afternoon. I suggest that it is this confusion which lies behind what is involved in this debate. The government, particularly the house leader and the Prime Minister, have a faulty notion of democracy and a veritable lust for efficiency; and related to both-in what causal sequence I do not know-is the strong desire for concentrated power in this government.
The essential purpose of the rules of the House of Commons is to maximize in a delicate balance the claims of democracy and the requirements of efficiency. The legitimate desire of the government is to rule effectively, and we must have procedures by which they will meet with considerable success. Ruling effectively, however, ceases to be legitimate when the opposition loses its effective right to oppose.
Already much has been said in this debate about the fact that the vast majority of the proposed changes in the rules are accepted, and indeed were proposed, by members on both sides of the house. Although a number of these changes will aid the opposition in its important task as critic of the government, I think it is true to say, and this bears emphasizing, that the effect of the majority of acceptable changes will be to enable the government to operate more efficiently.
In supporting these measures, therefore, the opposition has revealed in unmistakable terms its commitment to the progressive reform of the rules of the House of Commons. We in the New Democratic party believe that the important test of a government, apart from the question of democratic procedures in decision making, is how well it meets the needs and requirements of the Canadian people, what it is doing about housing, about a just system of taxation, about income redistribution, about regional economical disparities and the redistribution of power, about unemployment and about aid to developing nations. These are the very important questions that any government must be concerned about; and if for no other reason than to relieve the government of excuses, we would certainly like to see this debate come to an end so that they could get on and deal with these very serious matters.
What we have opposed is what the Leader of the Opposition and others have appropriately described as closure in advance. It seems to me to be completely irrelevant
whether or not closure in advance is to be found in other parliamentary systems. We have opposed and will continue to oppose, even if it is brought back to the committee, any form of standing order 16-A. By giving the government house leader the unilateral authority to set time limits in advance on the duration of debate on matters to be brought before us, we would be abandoning a crucial part of our democratic heritage. Again I repeat that I care not one whit whether other parliamentary systems have also abandoned it.
I suggested earlier that one of the tests of democratic decision making is that policies must be reached in the context of ample and open discussion. In recent years students of parliamentary government, from Bassett and Durbin to Jennings, Dawson and Macintosh, have indicated that in modem parliaments the opportunity to criticize government proposals is of fundamental importance and that what is crucially important is to maintain the strength of the opposition.
There is little hope for the opposition to get the government to make changes of substance in its proposals, but there is the possibility, and this is the serious question I think, of presenting to the public via parliamentary debate alternative views about policies and about kinds of societies.
There are two very important effects of this process of debate. First, it forces the government to reveal its reasons for acting. In doing this it also makes it more likely that government laws will be defensible laws, and government rules defensible rules. In short, this process makes it more likely that a governed country will be governed well. The second important consequence of this democratic process of public debate is that it enables a party with minority support to build, over a period of months or years, that minority into a majority. Only by having the time to show its ability in discussion can the rational foundation for belief in an opposition party as a credible alternative be established. Only arbitrary or authoritarian governments should be interested in denying or inhibiting this process.
However, this is exactly what the government will be doing if it uses its majority to force the proposed standing order 16-A upon us. Even if it is referred back to the committee, if it is the understanding of the government that rule 16-A will be revived once again, we cannot accept it. for rule 16-A or any other alternative form of the same procedure would turn parliament into a merely

December 19, 1968

consultative body before which the government would appear at intervals to seek formal ratification of its decisions. I suggest in all seriousness it would not in principle be unlike the supreme soviet in the Soviet Union. Debate would be of the most perfunctory kind. There would be pseudo discussion in a semi-democratic institution. We cannot permit this to happen, whether or not it has happened elsewhere. The only serious opposition in society would remain with the press, television and other outside organs of opinion. I repeat this is a very real possibility. Many serious students of government have suggested this has already happened to western democracy. It has been argued that the opposition no longer provides the serious criticism of government, but that it is provided by the press and other outside organs.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
On some matters the house leaders of all parties will be able to agree in advance that debate need not take long. But on many issues of public policy, the only rational way of deciding on the necessary time for discussion is in fact to let the debate proceed, to let the issue unfold itself, so to speak. Democrats from Pericles to John Stuart Mill have stressed the important fact that truth and significance can best be revealed in thorough and systematic discussion. Any issue may become a great issue during the process of debate. The voice of the people must be heard through their representatives on both sides of the house. The people, in turn, must be informed by means of the press, radio and television about what opponents of the government think is of significance.
On this point, Mr. Speaker, I am dismayed, for example, by the fact that no member of the Liberal party has risen to criticize the proposed standing order 16-A. Ever since the Labour party has been in power in Britain it has had one backbench revolt after another. When it formed the government the Conservative party in Great Britain had a number of backbench revolts on issues of concern to individual members. However, in this debate, not one Liberal member has stood up to criticize what his government is doing here. I find this very disturbing. Surely, it is not a unique ability of members of the opposition and the vast majority of newspaper writers in this country that enables them to see the dangers in 16-A. There must be a few Liberals around who also recognize these dangers. Perhaps the fact they do not voice their opinions further confirms the view that our government and
Motion for Concurrence in Report cabinet system have already become so centralized in the office of the Prime Minister that the backbench members on the government side unconsciously think it would be highly inappropriate for them to seriously oppose their government's policy.
I suggest that there is no essential connection between efficiency and democracy, but there is a relationship between efficiency and the concentration of power. I suggest that the man who is strongly tied to efficiency is also the man who is prone to concentrate power. The concentration of power is antithetical to democracy.
The proposed standing order 16-A is merely the most recent act of a government and Prime Minister assiduously pursuing technocratic efficiency. They are at the same time concentrating power. No serious person could possibly conclude otherwise.
If one talks to the majority of the academics across this country, most of whom supported the Liberals in the last election, he will ascertain how they feel. I suggest the Liberal backbenchers should conduct a survey of political science teachers across this country to see what they think of the Prime Minister these days.
Earlier in this session, the Prime Minister announced the cabinet roster system. By relieving cabinet ministers from the responsibility of being in the house each day to answer questions, two anti-democratic effects result. The first is that members of parliament have fewer opportunities to direct questions to all those responsible for governing. Second, the power of the Prime Minister is increased. Only the Prime Minister is here each day. This means that only he has the opportunity of keeping informed about all the interests and areas of concern of members of parliament, that is to say the interests of the Canadian people. This means, of course, that having day to day contact with the issues, and being the only member of cabinet acquainted with them, his position in cabinet must be immeasurably increased. He must have more power of persuasion, more influence over his fellow cabinet members. The roster system, then, is certainly a system that increases the power of the Prime Minister.
After the announcement of the roster system we learned that a series of regional desks was being established. Regional desks, a democrat might assume, would be set up so that the elected people most directly connected with the citizens of the country would

Motion for Concurrence in Report occupy those regional desks or have representation on them. But no, instead of those having the most direct access to the people being associated with the regional desks, we have the Prime Minister and only the Prime Minister having this direct contact. Once again, I would suggest that the power of the Prime Minister is thereby increased immeasurably, and will be in the future. We shall see that the power of members of parliament, those who are in most immediate contact with the people, will be further downgraded. Once again I suggest in all seriousness, in terms of our parliamentary system of government, that democracy has suffered a set-back in this country. If we had regional desks established on a proper basis, then members of parliament would occupy those regional desks, rather than the agents or representatives of the Prime Minister.
If there is a common factor linking the unrest in the western world amongst workers and students I suggest that common link, whether we are talking about students and workers in Czechoslovakia, whether we are talking about students and workers in France or students in North America, is a profound democratic movement in the world. This is true, whether our naive misguided government recognizes it or not. What is taking place is a very marked reaction to the concentration of power. This is true of the Czechs. It is true of young Frenchmen, it is true of young Canadians and young Americans in universities. I am sure this movement is going to affect us profoundly in the next two decades. It is something to which we should pay very close attention.
With the exception of the small elitist and non-liberal minority in its midst, it is something concerning which I think human beings in the mid-twentieth century should offer profound encouragement and profound praise. There is growing up a generation in all the industrial countries of the western world which has decided it is not going to accept irresponsible power, irresponsible authority, nor are its members even going to accept within a democratic society centres of highly concentrated power. They want it redistributed. This, I suggest, takes us back to the old, much more desirable form of democracy. I, for one, wish them every success.
It seems to me that it is within this particular social context of what is happening outside the House of Commons that we should be examining what is going on here. The pressures of the age are for a less rigid, more

open, more democratic and decentralized society.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
The pressures of the present government, however, are quite the opposite. Our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in the name of efficiency and democracy is concentrating power in his own office and in the cabinet, but more particularly in the former. His frequently commented upon discussions with young people do not, in my opinion, represent a shift to more democracy at all. These are pseudo-democratic symbols. At best they deceive some of the young into thinking that they have a direct influence upon the Prime Minister, though certainly none of the intelligent young to whom I have talked were taken in. However, a number are. At worst these discussions enable the Prime Minister, whether consciously or not, to manipulate both the young and the public at large. This is not what democracy is about; it is utterly ridiculous to think that it is.
To increase democracy is to decentralize decision making and to maximize free discussion, especially in institutions that have power.
If the Prime Minister wishes to reverse the authoritarian trend of his government, then he could make a good beginning by withdrawing, not only at the present time but even from future consideration, the proposed standing order 16-A. If he does not do so, then our party, and I am sure members of the other opposition parties, will continue with this profoundly important debate.

Mr. Speaker, there is no excuse for ignorance, and there is an example of it. In rising to take part in the debate on the motion before the house I would like first to associate myself with other hon. members on this side of the house, all of whom have stressed the obvious need for reform, and indeed our party's willingness to support and see adopted the vast majority of the reforms proposed. Again, Mr. Speaker, not unlike my colleagues I feel that there are certain proposed changes that, if adopted, will have the effects of destroying the essential functions of parliament, of destroying the effectiveness of our parliament especially the opposition's role which is an integral and important part of the constitutional organization of parliament.
Mr. Speaker, people across the country are shocked by what the government is trying to do in this motion. Newspaper comment has been unanimously critical. The government has made no case whatever for the necessity of measures that by their very nature are arbitrary, extreme and restrictive on parliament's freedom. This measure is designed for the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who sits in his seat, and when we raise questions that are of extreme importance to the province of Newfoundland, shrugs his shoulders and says "ditto." We cannot forget the fact that a few months ago in this house the Prime Minister said, "We are the masters." Now he wants to prove it, Mr. Speaker.
In my opinion, sir, if parliament is to be preserved as a living institution Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition must be able fearlessly to perform its functions. When it properly discharges them the preservation of our freedom is assured.
History, Mr. Speaker, has taught us that freedom always dies when criticism ends. I say now, sir, to the Prime Minister, to the members of the government and to all other Liberal members that you cannot, I repeat cannot, hold a stop watch on free speech. This, sir, I contend is what the government is aiming to do. It is aiming to hold a stop
December 19. 1968

Motion for Concurrence in Report watch on free speech, and I am telling them now it will not work.
According to the Prime Minister's own statements and the statements of other government spokesmen, what we are confronted with is an attempt by the government to control the procedures of parliament. Sir, I am sure it is a well known fact and established as one of the oldest traditions and the foundation of our freedom, that parliament controls its own procedures. I say to you, sir that a controlled parliament is not a free parliament. A controlled parliament is a mechanical toy for the government to play with. Sir, speaking as one member of this assembly, of this parliament, I say now that I was not, and indeed we were not elected to exercise that role. I will say this, sir, that if any hon. member of this house, on this side or on the government side, is prepared to accept that role he does not deserve the confidence and the trust that has been placed in him by the people. I say, Mr. Speaker, that he is not worthy of the honour to sit in this house and to be part of this great institution, the preservation of which has cost the lives of so many of our fellow Canadians.
Let me tell hon. members opposite, sir, that something more is at stake here than a mere question of procedure. What is at stake is the very essence and meaning of parliament. I ask you, are we to have an opposition that opposes, that is able to oppose a government, or are we to have an opposition whose hands are tied, an opposition gagged by the government? I don't think, Mr. Speaker, that this will work. In all fairness, sir, I don't think an opposition can function properly when it is gagged and its hands tied, unable to oppose because of rules imposed on this house.
I ask you, sir, are we to have a parliament that is free to talk or a parliament that is stifled before debate begins? I say to you, sir, that the government is attempting to produce a monster by a shotgun wedding between the American and the British systems. We must speak as men, Mr. Speaker, and we know that shotgun weddings do not usually work.
I suggest to you that the government, the Prime Minister and the house leader are proposing, as I have said, a shotgun wedding between the American and the British systems and, sir, it will not work. Our system has been developed over 100 years and has native attributes which cannot be compared with either of the other systems. In any case it should be neither one nor the other, and it certainly cannot be both.

[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
Every time there has been an erosion of freedom or thought, the excuse has been that this has been necessary to improve efficiency. The hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Blair) and the Prime Minister simply are the most recent editions in a long line of freedom eroders who use efficiency as an excuse for their actions. I say, sir, that what the government is proposing should be done by agreement and compromise. This is the only basis upon which a free parliament can function. If it is to be done by the government majority, used as an instrument to crush the opposition, then I feel there should be a full day's debate. I contend that the two hour limit is an insult to parliament. Parliament is not something that can be turned off and on like a tap. This house labours under sufficient handicaps now, when the Prime Minister and his ministers, after tying the hands of the house, run out and tell their stories before the television cameras. Even under our existing rules the Prime Minister today manages to do much of parliament's business outside the house.

I am sure hon. members will agree that hardly a night goes by when either the Prime Minister or some other ministers do not appear on national television to say unchallenged things they do not dare say in parliament where they would be challenged. It seems very strange to me that ministers who do not have to come in here and face questioning, because they are permitted to be away from the house on so many days in the week, are able to find the time to give their answers before the television cameras. I say that we now have a videotape government. It is a government that hides in isolation, with-the ministers appearing only when they are assured of preferential treatment. Is it any wonder that we cannot get any action on behalf of the Newfoundland fishing industry or in respect of the abandonment by the Canadian National Railways in Newfoundland?
A new principle has been written into the rules of parliament, and that new principle is one of government arrogance. Both the house leader and the Prime Minister are using the suggested need to put through a massive and beneficial program as a reason for butchering the rights of parliament. I ask the house leader, where is this program? It is not on the order paper. Does it exist only in the mind of the Prime Minister or in the mind of the
December 19, 1968	COMMONS
house leader? Why do they not list these measures in detail; why are they so secretive? I ask the Prime Minister, where is the promise of his just society? I have been told by people that there never has been such barren legislation on the order paper. I ask whether the house leader is reluctant to disclose the government's proposed legislation because he wants to change the rules first, paralyze parliament, and then bring in this rather mysterious legislation which they say they want but do not reveal?
As I have already stated, one of the oldest traditions and a foundation of our freedom is the assumption that parliament controls its own procedure. The second oldest principle is parliament's right to have grievances redressed prior to voting supply. The hon. member for Grenville-Carleton, who obviously has addressed himself to the task with a dedication worthy of a better cause, suggested that he would restore vigour to the supply procedures of this house. I ask him how this is possible, if supply is taken out of the house. The hon. member must know that grievances cannot be redressed in committees which are of an investigative nature, and not deliberative. These procedures remove from parliament the right to have grievances redressed. The purpose of supply and ways and means is, first, to examine and criticize the spending and taxing policies of the government. Second, and equally important, is the fact that it presents an opportunity to criticize the administration of government departments. One does not criticize in standing committees; one asks questions. We have lost the right to criticize as well as the right to voice opinions.
The government is asking the opposition to limit its own power to oppose. It is asking the government to gag parliament. If this bill is allowed to pass I contend that members of parliament will become dumb driven cattle, and parliament will be as obsolete as the pyramids. Parliament, sir, will be the tomb and not the defender of Canadian freedom.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday, December 9, I ask a supplementary question of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) as follows:
Does the government intend to include in the omnibus bill to amend the Criminal Code a measure abolishing corporal punishment?
The reason I asked that question was that I know from experience, more especially in criminal law, about the use of the broad strap and the cat-o'nine tails with regard to the treatment of men who have been sentenced and have had added to their sentence punishment by either the whip or the lash. I also learned that under the Penitentiary Act there is what is known as what the warden's court for discipline within the institution. In an article in the Toronto Daily Star of November 16, the writer, Mr. Earl McRae, set forth the concern of the executive director of the John Howard Society, Archibald Kirkpatrick, who has been interested in this problem for many years and had an interview with the reporter and set forth his views. His views are worthy of comment. He asked: What is the philosophy behind corporal punishment? The article then says:
"I think there's a strange Idea that the seat of emotions is in the seat of the pants," he says.
Most of the offences for which whipping can be included in the sentence are of a sexual nature, reflective, he says, of a disordered mind.
"Corporal punishment would not be considered appropriate in the treatment of mentally disturbed persons and therefore should not be considered in sex offences which are manifestly psychological in derivation," says Kirkpatrick.
"We have to change people's minds about corporal punishment. They say it is similar to chastising a child. But, when you chastise a child it is done out of love in a home of love. It is
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion accepted in this context. When you whip or strap a grown man you are depriving him of a great deal of his dignity and humanity. We are negating all evidence of humanistic behaviour in modern society. If a man commits an offence, we should be finding out what makes him do these things. We should be trying to rehabilitate him. Corporal punishment, in my mind, is simply vengeance."
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
In this article he goes on to set forth the views of an assistant warden of Kingston penitentiary who said:
-last year, about a dozen inmates received the whip or strap.
"And, I don't like it at all", he said. "None of us do, believe me."
"I have an aversion to it, every officer in here has. We try to preserve as much human dignity as possible. We don't want to look like a bunch of brutes."
The warden said "It seems to have an effect" for short periods on a few inmates "but morally, I am against it."
Then we have the report of one of the staff doctors, Dr. W. T. Amodeo who said with regard to the effects of corporal punishment:
"No, I don't think it effects any kind of reformation," he told The Star. "I don't think it is of any value at all.
As a result of that article I directed some remarks to the commissioner of penitentiaries when he appeared before the standing committee on justice and legal affairs. The parliamentary secretary nods his head to show that he remembers that occasion. I said to the commissioner, A. J. MacLeod:
Mr. Commissioner, I would like to direct other questions to you with regard to corporal punishment. Under the Code you have the whipping section, section 641, with which you are probably familiar, and I understand there are two types of whipping, the lash and the broad strap. Could you tell me how many inmates received corporal punishment in the last three years?
He set forth the two types, the type that is imposed by the judge and the type that is imposed under the warden's court. Then he said:
I have that information somewhere here. Corporal punishment as a sentence of an institutional board of discipline in our institutions was handed down once this year between January 1 and the middle of October; 19 times in 1967; 32 times in 1966; 7 times in 1965; 26 times in 1964.
So you can see that in this last year only one person has been administered corporal punishment as a result of the warden's court decision. Then he gave the figures with regard to sentences by judges and he said:
-8 times so far this year, from January to the middle of October; 5 in 1967; 3 in 1966; 3 in 1965; 22 in 1964 ; 9 in 1963.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it was about a week and a half ago that a number of members in this house, including myself, raised the question with the government about whether, particularly having in mind the Christmas season, the old age security pension cheques could not be mailed out a little bit early to their recipients. My question was ruled out of order by Mr. Speaker, and I welcome the opportunity of restating it tonight. I think the reasoning of members in this connection was that it would cost the taxpayers and the government no more money to do this, and it would help the old age pensioners, particularly those on small fixed incomes such as the old age pension itself, to have a little better Christmas than otherwise. I felt therefore this was a reasonable request, and I still think so.
I was pleased myself today to receive my cheque from the government approximately a week and a half ahead of time in the amount of approximately $2,200. This of course includes our quarterly expenses. I was glad to get this, particularly at this time of year, and it does not cost the government any more money to give us this ahead of time. If I was glad to have $2,000 today a little ahead of time, I would think the old age pensioners of this country, numbering about half a million and who receive from this government only about $75 or $80 per month, would be even more pleased to get their cheques ahead of time.
I am not saying this in any demogogic way; I think it is a matter of common sense. It is reasonable that if members of parliament receive their cheques ahead of time, then the old age pensioners, even although it is late in the month, should receive theirs ahead of time. I hope the government, even now, will consider speeding up the delivery of old age pensioners' monthly cheques. I sincerely hope that the government will not give the same old answer, that the senior citizens of this country-who are 75 or 85 years of age-are so inexperienced that as soon as they get the money a week ahead of time they will be throwing it around and
December 19. 1968

living it up. On $18 to $19 a week surely that is ridiculous.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
As I say, this step would not cost the public any more money. I am glad to see the Liberal members here tonight, thus indicating some support for this question. Therefore I again ask why the government will not take this action and mail out the cheques, even at this date, so as to give the old age pensioners and senior citizens a little bit of a break.
